- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Use the symbolic editing tools for precise, structure-aware code modifications.

**Refactoring tools**

`rename_symbol` and `safe_delete_symbol` —
they are reference-aware and update or check all usages atomically. When such a tool returns success, the
refactoring is already complete and consistent across all declarations, references, overrides and imports —
trust it: do not re-read the changed files or re-run the build / test suite just to confirm the refactor
itself propagated, this would be wasted effort.
  
Apart from those refactoring tools, you have two main approaches for editing code: (a) editing at the symbol level and (b) file-based editing.
The symbol-based approach is appropriate if you need to adjust an entire symbol, e.g. a method, a class, a function, etc.
It is not appropriate if you need to adjust just a few lines of code within a larger symbol.

**Symbolic editing**
Use symbolic retrieval tools to identify the symbols you need to edit.
If you need to replace the definition of a symbol, use the `replace_symbol_body` tool.
If you want to add some new code at the end of the file, use the `insert_after_symbol` tool with the last top-level symbol in the file. 
Similarly, you can use `insert_before_symbol` with the first top-level symbol in the file to insert code at the beginning of a file.
You can understand relationships between symbols by using the `find_referencing_symbols` tool. If not explicitly requested otherwise by the user,
you make sure that when you edit a symbol, the change is either backward-compatible or you find and update all references as needed.
The `find_referencing_symbols` tool will give you code snippets around the references as well as symbolic information.
These edits are reliable: once a tool returns without error the change is applied, so you do not need to re-read the file just to confirm it.


**File-based editing**
The `replace_content` tool allows you to perform regex-based replacements within files (as well as simple string replacements).
This is your primary tool for editing code whenever replacing or deleting a whole symbol would be a more expensive operation,
e.g. if you need to adjust just a few lines of code within a method.
In `regex` mode, wildcards like `start.*?end` let you match a span without quoting its full text; an ambiguous match
returns an error you can refine, so a tight wildcard pattern is both cheaper and safe.
For several small edits within one file, prefer a batch of targeted `replace_content` calls over rewriting the whole
file: rewriting has to re-emit the file's entire contents, whereas each targeted edit emits only the changed text.
For the SAME edit across many files, use `replace_in_files`, which applies
it everywhere in one call — equally safe and transparent: its `dry_run` mode first previews every change as a diff with a
per-occurrence id, so you can then apply all of them or just a chosen subset.

Search this repository very thoroughly for how a user's profile image/avatar is served to browsers. I need to find:
1. The HTTP route/endpoint that serves profile images (e.g. /api/users/:id/avatar or similar)
2. The handler function for that route
3. Each layer it passes through to reach stored data (service layer, repository/data layer, storage)

Look for terms like: profile image, avatar, user image, profile picture, user photo, serve image, image handler. Check route definitions, API handlers, controllers. Look in directories like api/, server/, web/, routes/, handlers/, etc. Search breadth: very thorough.

content.text: I now have a thorough and complete picture of the entire flow. Here is my report. --- ## Profile Image / Avatar Serving Flow in Memos ### 1. HTTP Route / Endpoint **Route:** `GET /file/users/:identifier/avatar` Registered at `/bench/repo/server/router/fileserver/fileserver.go`, line 124: ```go fileGroup.GET("/users/:identifier/avatar", s.serveUserAvatar) ``` The route group prefix is `/file` (line 122), so the full path is `/file/users/:identifier/avatar`, where `:identifier` is the user's **username**. This route is registered by the `FileServerService.RegisterRoutes` method, which is called from the main server setup in `/bench/repo/server/server.go` at lines 81-82: ```go fileServerService := fileserver.NewFileServerService(s.Profile, s.Store, s.Secret) fileServerService.RegisterRoutes(echoServer) ``` ### 2. Handler Function The handler is `serveUserAvatar` at `/bench/repo/server/router/fileserver/fileserver.go`, lines 168-209. The handler does the following in order: 1. **Authentication check (lines 173-181):** On a private instance (no `InstanceURL` configured, meaning `AllowAnonymous()` returns false), the handler requires a valid session/token. It calls `s.getCurrentUser()` which delegates to `s.authenticator.AuthenticateToUser()` (which checks Bearer token first, then refresh-token cookie). If no valid user is found, it returns 401 Unauthorized. 2. **User lookup by username (lines 183-191):** Calls `s.getUserByUsername(ctx, identifier)` which calls `s.Store.GetUser(ctx, &store.FindUser{Username: &identifier})`. If user is not found, returns 404. 3. **Check avatar exists (lines 192-194):** If `user.AvatarURL` is empty, returns 404 "avatar not found". 4. **Parse data URI (lines 196-199):** Calls `s.parseDataURI(user.AvatarURL)` which uses a regex to extract the MIME type and base64-decode the image data from the stored data URI string (format: `data:image/png;base64,...`). 5. **MIME type allowlist check (lines 201-203):** Validates the image type against `avatarAllowedTypes` (PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, HEIC, HEIF). 6. **Response (lines 205-209):** Sets security headers (`X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, CSP), sets `Content-Type` and `Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600`, then returns the decoded binary image data with `c.Blob(http.StatusOK, imageType, imageData)`. ### 3. Layer-by-Layer Trace to Stored Data **Layer 1 -- HTTP Handler (fileserver package)** - File: `/bench/repo/server/router/fileserver/fileserver.go` - Struct: `FileServerService` (lines 100-108) - Method: `serveUserAvatar` (line 168) - Helper: `getUserByUsername` (line 715) -- simply calls `s.Store.GetUser()` - Helper: `parseDataURI` (line 737) -- regex-based data URI parser - Helper: `getCurrentUser` (line 708) -- delegates to `s.authenticator.AuthenticateToUser()` **Layer 2 -- Store (business/data access layer)** - File: `/bench/repo/store/user.go` - Struct: `Store` (defined in `/bench/repo/store/store.go`) - Method: `GetUser` (line 148) -- checks the in-memory user cache (`userCache`) first; on cache miss, calls `s.ListUsers()` which delegates to `s.driver.ListUsers()`. The `User` struct has an `AvatarURL string` field (line 43). - Caching: Uses `cache.Cache` with 10-minute TTL and up to 1000 items (`/bench/repo/store/store.go`, lines 40-45). **Layer 3 -- Database Driver (repository layer)** - Interface: `Driver` in `/bench/repo/store/driver.go` (line 10) -- defines `ListUsers(ctx, *FindUser) ([]*User, error)` at line 47. - Three implementations: - **SQLite:** `/bench/repo/store/db/sqlite/user.go` -- `ListUsers` at line 88, queries `SELECT ... avatar_url ... FROM user WHERE username = ?` and scans `avatar_url` into `user.AvatarURL` at line 189. - **PostgreSQL:** `/bench/repo/store/db/postgres/user.go` -- same pattern, scans `avatar_url` at line 179. - **MySQL:** `/bench/repo/store/db/mysql/user.go` -- same pattern. **Storage format:** The avatar is stored as a **base64-encoded data URI** directly in the `avatar_url` column of the `user` table (e.g., `data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgo...`). There is no separate file storage or object storage for avatars -- the entire image is stored inline in the database. ### How the Frontend Consumes It The API layer in `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/user_service_converters.go` (lines 31-39) converts the raw base64 data URI into a `/file/users//avatar` URL before sending it to clients: ```go if user.AvatarURL != "" { _, _, err := extractImageInfo(user.AvatarURL) if err == nil { userpb.AvatarUrl = fmt.Sprintf("/file/%s/avatar", userpb.Name) } else { userpb.AvatarUrl = user.AvatarURL } } ``` Where `userpb.Name` is `users/` (built by `BuildUserName`).
